title: 5 Signs You Have AuDHD (ADHD and Autism)

segments.text: If you have ever felt like your brain is caught
in a tug-of-war between wanting structure,
and then actively rebelling against it,
or your thoughts are going
100 miles per hour constantly
but you also need longer  processing time than other people,
especially in conversations,
or you process it days or months later.
Hey Debby, I think I got it!
Well, you just might be an autistic ADHDer
or an AuDHDer.
And let me tell you, having  both together in one brain
is absolutely insane.
So today we're breaking down 5 signs it's AUDHD.
Because why have just ONE  neurotype when you can have
TWO that directly contradict each other.
Constantly.
Let's get into it.
Number 1
You create a million tasks
and then get paralyzed by the overwhelm.
Today's your day to get organized.
You sit down, make a beautiful to-do list,
maybe even color code it.
Add a few sticky notes,
or dozens of sticky notes,
and while you're at it you'll just jot down
a few other projects you've  been meaning to get to.
Oh, but those mean extra steps,
picking up supplies.
Okay, write it down. There you go.
Step back and
oh oh
for a moment everything feels possible
until your brain catches up to the tasks
and what you just assigned yourself.
Now you realize just how many steps are involved.
Ah, why would someone think  you could do that much?
Wait.
Wa-was that me?
Now you're running back to your bed.
Need to hide from the Attack of the List
that's clearly out to get you
or to make sure you don't even start
because how can you start  when there's so much involved
and you're feeling really, really shy.
It's the ultimate contradiction.
You want to do things.
You usually keep yourself really busy,
but your ADHD brain is often  jumping from task to task
because they're all important
and so is the deep research you're now doing
on the absolute best cleaning  system for oak tables.
Uh, and how about that original task list?
Don't ask that.
That seems like a pointed question.
But does much get done?
Uh, sometimes.
Not if another thing pops up in the middle that
pulls you elsewhere.
But you had to go down that rabbit hole.
You needed the information
before you can continue to the next thing.
Wait, what was the next thing?
There are too many things.
Ah, so many things.
And where to begin?
Now you're overwhelmed.
It's too much.
Retreat to the bed and hide.
And by the way, where did this mess come from?
Your autistic brain will often hate any clutter.
Clutter in the brain or in your space.
The trick is keeping things manageable
based on what works for you.
Like making a list
of your top three things  to accomplish for the day.
Small things, parts of larger tasks,
not something like clean the house
because that in itself could become so much more
than a day of cleaning.
So, something like clean the living room.
That'll give you a short purpose and clear goals.
Less chance of overwhelm  and a way to start quickly.
Get that win, which both  parts of your brain will love.
Number 2
You crave routine, but also  fight it every step of the way.
There's something comforting about structure,
especially for autistic brains.
Predictability makes life  easier, reduces decision fatigue,
and helps avoid that feeling
of floating through space with no direction.
But the second you tell yourself  you have to do something,
your brain goes
"Actually no."
And now let me play that conversation
that happened 17 years ago on repeat.
Bedtime is a classic.
You know you function better with sleep.
You set a bedtime.
You have a plan for the next day
that hinges on getting sleep,
but now that it's a scheduled thing or a rule.
well, if you're autistic and also have ADHD
and especially if you have the PDA profile
you probably feel like the rule makes it something
you particularly don't like.
You know you need it, but  doing it feels like a demand,
and you don't like demands.
It feels too restrictive, even when you're the one
making the demand.
And then add in your super-active ADHD brain
and now it's 2 a.m and you're  watching your 10th video
on how to create earthen bricks
using the soil on your own land
with machines that you don't have
on land that you don't own yet.
So you know you need routines and predictability,
especially to keep your autistic brain
from having meltdowns constantly.
But you also actively create  ways to not keep the routine.
And your ADHD brain loves spontaneity,
like deep diving into new  interests when it's bedtime,
or sporadically booking a trip
when, actually, you don't sleep well anywhere
except your own bed.
The best way to help your brain?
Flexible routines.
Instead of
"I must sleep at 11:00 p.m,"
it's
"I get into bed around 8:00 p.m
and then I start winding down."
Enough structure with enough freedom
so your brain doesn't rebel.
And if you want a visual
with more key traits of autism and ADHD
so you can really visualize all the chaos
that's going on in there,
we've got a free download in the description.
Now back to the list.
Number 3
You want to be around people  until you actually are.
Socializing sounds great in theory.
You get the urge to be around people.
You make plans, and for the  first 20 minutes, it's fun.
And then, your social battery drains instantly.
The irony? Sometimes it's actually you,
your idea, your setup, your plans.
In one of those moments of ADHD impulsivity.
So you might even be in your  house with these friends,
but now they're all here in your space
and you need to hide.
This is one reason why the holiday season
can be especially draining  for neurodivergent people,
and especially for autistic ADHDers.
It's excitement and wanting  to be around people you love
and simultaneously wanting to  hide for the next 6 months.
So when you have those social urges,
but you feel paralyzed by the realization
that being around people takes so much energy,
you go from excited to exhausted in minutes.
So then, you're desperately trying to get a break
without being weird about it.
Or, you're zoning out because you're overwhelmed
and shutting down, or interrupting  because you want to say
what you want to say and  ADHD impulsivity pushes you
to get it out there.
And mix in the autistic tendency
not to get social cues exactly right
for knowing when to jump in,
and before you know it,
you've interrupted for the fifth time.
And what can you do?
Well, if you're like me, the  only way to go, is forward.
So you're fully-engaged, oversharing, info-dumping
and carrying the whole conversation.
You're a one man show telling everyone
about your earth and brick house design plans
with a stone foundation, a thermal mass wall,
and a shark tank.
The glossed-over looks start.
So then, you're slowing down, crashing mentally,
and it's only been 20 minutes.
I mean you do like these  people, but you need an escape.
Yes, it was your idea, but how did you forget
that socializing drains your  mostly depleted autistic battery
faster than basically anything else.
What's really happening here?
Where can I go?
How long could I be in the bathroom
before someone sends for help?
So the best way to handle it?
Pre-planned breaks.
Give yourself an out,
like a break by going and prepping some snacks,
or cleaning up some dishes,
Or if you're out instead of at home,
say you need to take a call outside,
and then just get some fresh air,
and a few minutes of quiet.
Number 4
You love the idea of being out and about
until sensory overload takes over.
Getting out of the house,
or a familiar setting like your workplace,
might feel like a great plan.
Maybe you're going to a new coffee shop
to get work done with a colleague.
Seems like a great idea, right?
A nice cafe, a little background noise,
and productivity mode ON.
ADHD loves the stimulation.
New environment, people-watching,  something different.
So you get there, and for the  first few minutes, it's great.
Then suddenly it's all too much.
The espresso machine is making  horrible screeching sounds.
The chairs are weirdly uncomfortable.
There's an air conditioning unit that hums
at exactly the wrong frequency.
And why is the barista acting  like he's working the ER?
The stress seeping out of this  dude is impacting the vibes.
Now that you think about it, why does it seem like
everything is happening everywhere, all at once?
So suddenly, your brain is spending all its energy
just processing the environment,
instead of actually doing any work.
Every clang of a dish, or peel of sudden laughter,
these all feel like an onslaught.
And no, you can't just tune them out
with noise-cancelling headphones
when you also need to occasionally  chat with your colleague,
which means that now your autistic brain
is screaming for an escape,
while the ADHD side still wants to power through.
ADHD brain, don't do something weird.
It's not that bad.
Is that John Mayer playing?
Did I order nachos?
Nope.
No distractions for autistic brain.
It's already halfway into shutdown mode,
regretting every life choice  that led to this moment.
So you can't focus, you can't  relax, and you're caught
in a battle between
"let's keep it going"
and
"if I don't leave immediately I might explode."
The fix?
Know your sensory limits.
If working in a cafe sounds fun,
but always turns into a disaster,
a quiet corner at home or a familiar spot
might be the better option.
And learn to recognize when  sensory limits are approaching
before they hit full overload,
but also giving yourself permission to leave
when your brain says enough,
because it's tiring enough  having the pull in your brain,
but then if you feel like you have to explain.
It's often too much.
Number 5
Your energy levels are wildly inconsistent.
Some days you feel unstoppable.
You're hyper-productive, multitasking like a pro,
and your brain is on fire.
And then the next day, you crash so hard
it's like you've been hit by a truck,
with a snow plow.
Your body needs rest, but ADHD brain is screaming
"We should keep going! We  got 25 things to do today."
An autistic brain is just  overwhelmed by ADHD brain,
and exhaustion from whatever made you crash
in the first place.
And life in general, because  being autistic is stressful.
So how does this look?
You're probably someone who looks like they have
frequent mood swings and massive energy changes,
especially across days and weeks.
And a lot of that is because  there really is a war going on
in your head and body.
ADHD thrives on movement and activity,
constantly seeking dopamine.
It pushes you to do things by being impulsive
and always, always moving.
The autistic side needs  recovery time and structure,
and seeing things through to completion.
This is especially true after socializing,
over-stimulation, or overexertion,
which happens a lot
when you have ADHD mixed in there.
And for me, ADHD tends to be louder.
So it convinces me to go do that thing,
to keep going, keep pushing through,
until my autistic brain hits  a full meltdown or shutdown
because I've ignored my limits for too long.
And then it's a complete and  fairly horrible experience
when the autistic brain really pushes back.
Sometimes where I'm in bed for hours,
or even days,
because I am so exhausted.
It's really like my autistic  brain hits the brakes hard.
And this often comes with physical symptoms.
So what can you do?
Recognize when your body needs rest
before it forces you to stop.
If your brain is in go-go-go mode,
but you're also feeling the pull  from your body or your brain,
you pause and hear it saying,
"Whoa there buddy! Let's hold off a bit."
Listen to it.
"Good god man Listen to me."
Finding a balance between activity and recovery
is hard for everyone,
especially with how fast-paced  today's world often is.
But when you're neurodivergent,
ignoring it will only make things worse.
And anyone with autism-ADHD combo will know
the other hard truth.
We're used to pushing through exhaustion,
being told we need to try harder,
being told it's us.
And it's what often leads  to burnout, chronic stress,
and exhaustion.
And more.
But it's not that something is wrong with us.
It's that our brains have a lot  happening behind the scenes,
and only we know it.
So that's why we have to work with our brains
to figure out our needs in  order to help ourselves,
not just survive, but thrive.
So if any of this sounded familiar,
let me know in the comments.
Which one got you the most?
And if you have your own AuDHD signs to add,
I want to hear them.
